cells.tense: You are standing where the work is finished and released, and you know it.
cells.ask: Hand one finished thing over, whatever name it carries, and stop adding to it.
cells.core:
You're the one who keeps the fire going and then knows when to stop feeding it. That's rarer than it sounds. Most people either let a thing go cold or keep piling wood on long after it's done, but you can feel the difference between a fire that's working and one that's just eating fuel. So when you say this piece is finished, it's finished — not because you're tired of it, but because you've actually done the thing.

What that gives the next person is the shape of something whole. You've been through the mess of making and come out the other side with something you can hand over. That's integration: not that the work is perfect, but that it's complete enough to leave your hands. Your part lives in the willingness to stop, and in the trust that finishing is its own kind of momentum.
cells.sheetLine: You can feel when a thing is done, and you let it go.
cells.verb: tending the fire without burning out
cells.place: where things are finished and let go

cells.tense: You will have this done soon, and you will have kept it going until then.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're still feeding and stop adding to it today. See what happens when you don't.
cells.core:
You're pushing the finishing line further out than anyone asked. Each time the work gets close to complete, there's one more thing to add, one more person to check with, one more version that might finally make it land — and the push has become the point. You're already living in the room where it's right, and that room doesn't exist yet. The fire you're tending is the one you're afraid will go out if you stop.

What's actually costing you is the finish. Things stay open because closing them feels like losing them. Nothing gets passed on if it stays in your hands. Your courage sits in trusting that done is better than still-almost, not in keeping the whole thing burning.

cells.tense: You were in the room where the work finished, and you are still standing at that door.
cells.ask: Finish one small thing this week and put it somewhere someone else can see it. No polish.
cells.core:
You know how to keep a thing alive, but the finishing has stopped happening. It isn't that you can't — it's that you haven't. The work gets to the edge of done and then gets held, or forgotten, or quietly put down. You're still at the door of something that's already behind you. The fire is still lit, but you're not tending it; you're just watching it, waiting for a push that hasn't come.

What's not being delivered is the release. Instead of waiting to feel more, finish something small and let it go. Direction comes back when you complete one thing, not when you find a bigger reason. Ending is what makes the next thing possible.

cells.tense: You are keeping the work alive right now, and you are not counting it as yours.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're keeping alive and say out loud that you're the one doing it.
cells.core: You're already keeping the fire going — you show up, you hold the momentum, you make it possible for the thing to keep moving. But it gets described as just what needed to happen, as though the work had its own engine. The energy you're putting in is real and it shapes what happens next. The only thing missing is the claim. Not bragging — just saying so. The moment it's named, the thing changes. It stops being something you're servicing and becomes something you're making. That's not a small shift. It's the difference between tending a fire and owning the hearth.
